steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on CWTM, a neural topic model that uses contextualized word embeddings from BERT instead of bag-of-words input. Cover the limitations of existing topic models, the motivation for using pre-trained language models, our approach, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Topic modeling and the bag-of-words limitation
- Static word embeddings and topic-specific embeddings in topic models
- Pre-trained language models and contextualized word embeddings
- Existing topic models built on pre-trained LMs and their gaps
- Our approach
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Topic modeling and BOW
  - explores latent themes in large document collections; document = mixture of topics; topic = word list sorted by co-occurrence association strength
  - most models (probabilistic or neural) rely on BOW, as training input or target
  - BOW encodes documents by word occurrence; ignores syntactic/semantic relations -> limits topic coherence
- Word embeddings in topic models
  - some incorporate pre-trained word embeddings for syntactic/semantic info; but same word = identical embedding regardless of context
  - others jointly learn topics + topic-specific word embeddings; don't use pre-trained LMs
- Pre-trained LMs
  - BERT, T5, GPT -> new era of NLP
  - distinct contextualized embedding per occurrence of a word
  - better than static embeddings for word sense disambiguation; better with OOV words; meaningful representations for rare/unseen words
  - improve text classification, NER, QA
- Topic models with pre-trained LMs
  - CTM: contextual info from BERT, good performance; but only document embeddings, still BOW inputs -> misses contextualized word embeddings, OOV issue
  - other work: topics from pre-trained LMs as a clustering task -> hard to integrate with downstream NLP tasks
- Our approach
  - novel neural topic model combining contextualized word embeddings from BERT
  - assumption: words with different semantic meanings have different topic info
  - encode topic info directly from contextualized word embeddings -> more coherent, meaningful topics; handles unseen words in newly arrived documents
  - map each BERT contextualized word embedding to latent topic vector; aggregate to represent topics
  - document-topic vectors = weighted average pooling of word-topic vectors in same document
- Contributions
  - (1) CWTM, no BOW assumption; mitigates OOV
  - (2) compared with LDA and other neural topic models on five datasets; more coherent, meaningful topics
  - (3) word-topic vectors improve downstream tasks e.g. NER -> semantically meaningful

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Topic modeling is widely used to explore latent themes in large document collections. Each document is modeled as a mixture of topics, and each topic is a list of words sorted by how strongly they are associated with the topic by co-occurrence. Most existing topic models, both probabilistic and neural network based, rely on bag-of-words (BOW) information, either as the input during training or as the training target. BOW representations just encode each document by which words occur in it. This ignores the syntactic and semantic relationships between words, and so it limits how coherent the topics produced by topic models can be.

Some topic models use pre-trained word embeddings to get syntactic and semantic information, but they still cannot capture the contextual meaning of a word well, because the same word always has the same word embedding no matter what its context is. Some other topic models learn topics and topic-specific word embeddings jointly to address this, but they do not use the advantages of pre-trained language models.

With pre-trained language models like BERT, T5 and GPT, natural language processing (NLP) research entered a new era. These models capture the context around each word, so they generate a different contextualized word embedding for each occurrence of a word in a text. Contextualized word embeddings are better than static word embeddings for word sense disambiguation, because they capture the contextual nuances of how a word is used. They are also better at handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. Since they are generated from context, they give meaningful representations for rare or unseen words. Research has shown that they improve the performance of many NLP tasks, including text classification, named entity recognition and question answering.

- Topic models with pre-trained LMs
  - CTM: contextual info from BERT, good performance; but only document embeddings + still BOW inputs -> no contextualized word embeddings, OOV issue
  - other work learns topics from pre-trained LMs as clustering -> hard to integrate with downstream tasks
- Our approach
  - neural topic model combining contextualized word embeddings from BERT; words with different meanings carry different topic info
  - more coherent/meaningful topics; handles unseen words from newly arrived documents
  - word embedding -> latent topic vector, aggregated into topics; document-topic vectors via weighted average pooling of word-topic vectors
- Contributions: (1) CWTM, no BOW, mitigates OOV; (2) vs LDA and neural topic models, five datasets; (3) word-topic vectors help downstream tasks e.g. NER

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Topic modeling is widely used to explore latent themes in large document collections. Each document is modeled as a mixture of topics, and each topic is a list of words sorted by how strongly they are associated with the topic by co-occurrence. Most existing topic models, both probabilistic and neural network based, rely on bag-of-words (BOW) information, either as the input during training or as the training target. BOW representations just encode each document by which words occur in it. This ignores the syntactic and semantic relationships between words, and so it limits how coherent the topics produced by topic models can be.

Some topic models use pre-trained word embeddings to get syntactic and semantic information, but they still cannot capture the contextual meaning of a word well, because the same word always has the same word embedding no matter what its context is. Some other topic models learn topics and topic-specific word embeddings jointly to address this, but they do not use the advantages of pre-trained language models.

With pre-trained language models like BERT, T5 and GPT, natural language processing (NLP) research entered a new era. These models capture the context around each word, so they generate a different contextualized word embedding for each occurrence of a word in a text. Contextualized word embeddings are better than static word embeddings for word sense disambiguation, because they capture the contextual nuances of how a word is used. They are also better at handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. Since they are generated from context, they give meaningful representations for rare or unseen words. Research has shown that they improve the performance of many NLP tasks, including text classification, named entity recognition and question answering.

Topic models can also use the advantages of pre-trained language models. The Contextualized Topic Model (CTM) uses contextual information from BERT and gets good performance. But it only uses contextual information from document embeddings and still uses BOW representations as training inputs, so it misses the benefits of contextualized word embeddings and has the OOV issue. Several other works also propose learning topics from pre-trained language models, but they treat topic modeling as a clustering task, which makes it hard to integrate them with other downstream NLP tasks.

In our work, we developed a new neural topic model that combines contextualized word embeddings from BERT. We assume that words with different semantic meanings have different topic information. We show that if topic information is encoded directly from contextualized word embeddings, our model can produce more coherent and meaningful topics, and it can also handle unseen words in newly arrived documents. Specifically, we map each contextualized word embedding from BERT to a latent topic vector, and we aggregate these vectors to represent topics. The document-topic vectors are obtained by weighted average pooling of the word-topic vectors in the same document.

Our contributions are three-fold: (1) We developed a new neural topic model, CWTM, which integrates contextualized word embeddings from BERT and does not rely on the BOW assumption. Our model effectively mitigates the OOV issue. (2) We compared our model with Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and other neural topic models on five datasets and showed that it produces more coherent and meaningful topics. (3) We showed that the word-topic vectors learned by our model can improve the performance of downstream tasks such as named entity recognition, which means the vectors are semantically meaningful.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Topic modeling has been widely used to explore latent themes within large document collections, where each document is modeled as a mixture of topics, and a topic is represented by a list of words sorted by their co-occurrence association strength with the topic. Most existing topic models, whether probabilistic or neural network based, rely on bag-of-words (BOW) information, either as input during training or as the target for training. BOW representations simply encode each document based on word occurrence within the document. This ignores syntactic and semantic relationships between words, thus limiting the ability of topic models to produce more coherent topics.

While some topic models incorporate pre-trained word embeddings to capture syntactic and semantic information [1,2,3,4,5,6], they still fall short in capturing the contextual meaning of a word, as the same word shares an identical word embedding irrespective of its surrounding context. Although some other topic models jointly learn topics and topic-specific word embeddings [7,8,9] to address this limitation, they do not leverage the advantages of pre-trained language models.

With the development of pre-trained language models like BERT [10], T5 [11], and GPT [12], natural language processing (NLP) research has entered a new era. By capturing the surrounding context of each word, these models generate distinct contextualized word embeddings for each occurrence of a word in text. Contextualized word embeddings are superior to static word embeddings for word sense disambiguation, as they capture the contextual nuances of word usage. They also show improved capability in handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words [13,14]: because they are generated contextually, they offer meaningful representations for rare or unseen words. Research has shown that they enhance the performance of various NLP tasks, including text classification, named entity recognition, and question answering [10,11,12].

Topic models can also leverage the advantages of pre-trained language models. The Contextualized Topic Model (CTM) [15] incorporates contextual information from BERT and achieves good performance. However, it only integrates contextual information from document embeddings and still relies on BOW representations as training inputs, thus missing out on the benefits of contextualized word embeddings and suffering from the OOV issue. [16], [17] and [18] also propose learning topics from pre-trained language models, but they treat topic modeling as a clustering task, which makes seamless integration with other downstream NLP tasks challenging.

In our work, we developed a novel neural topic model combining contextualized word embeddings from BERT [10]. We assume that words with different semantic meanings have different topic information, and show that by encoding topic information directly from contextualized word embeddings, our model can produce more coherent and meaningful topics, while also being capable of handling unseen words from newly arrived documents. Specifically, we map each contextualized word embedding from BERT to a latent topic vector and aggregate these vectors to represent topics. The document-topic vectors are represented by applying weighted average pooling to the word-topic vectors in the same document.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold: (1) We have developed a novel neural topic model called the Contextlized Word Topic Model (CWTM), which integrates contextualized word embeddings from BERT without relying on the BOW assumption, and effectively mitigates the OOV issue. (2) We have compared our model with Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and other neural topic models across five datasets and shown that it produces more coherent and meaningful topics. (3) We have shown that the word-topic vectors learned by our model can improve the performance of downstream tasks such as named entity recognition, indicating that the vectors are semantically meaningful.
